title.rendered: How to Change Fonts on iPhone: Easy Tips Without Jailbreaking

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • The Main Limitation: You cannot change the default system font on iOS, but you can install new fonts for supported apps.
  • System-Wide Adjustments: While you can’t change the font style, you can adjust text size and boldness system-wide for readability.
  • In-App Customization: Apps like Pages, Keynote, and Mail allow you to change fonts and text styles within them.
  • Installing Custom Fonts: Install custom fonts for use in compatible apps using dedicated font apps from the App Store.
  • Managing Fonts: Manage or remove installed custom fonts at any time via the Settings app to revert to default.

Changing the font on your iPhone can make your device feel more personal and easier to read. Unfortunately, Apple doesn’t let you change the system-wide font, but you can still tweak it in specific apps, adjust text size, or use third-party apps for more options. This article walks you through all the safe and easy ways to change the font on your iPhone.

Table of Contents
  • Why You Might Want to Change Fonts on iPhone
  • Understanding Font Limitations in iOS
  • How to Change Font Size in iPhone Settings
    • How to Make Text Bold and Adjust Display Contrast
  • How to Use Fonts in Notes, Pages, and Mail
    • Customize Font Style in Notes App
    • Change Font Style in Apple Pages
    • Change Font Style in Mail App (iOS 26+)
  • How to Install Custom Fonts on iPhone
    • Method 1: Install Fonts from iPhone Settings
    • Method 2: Use Font Installer Apps
    • Method 3: Use Configuration Profiles with iFont
  • How to Use Custom Fonts in Third-Party Apps
    • How to Change Keyboard Fonts on iPhone
  • Best Font Apps for iPhone in 2025
  • Troubleshooting Font Installation Issues
  • How to Manage and Remove Fonts on iPhone
  • How to Revert to the Default Font
  • Final Thoughts

Why You Might Want to Change Fonts on iPhone

Fonts play a big role in how you interact with your iPhone. Here are some reasons to customize them:

  • Personalization: A unique font can reflect your style, making your iPhone feel like yours. 
  • Readability: Larger fonts can make text clearer and easier to read. 
  • Creativity: Custom fonts in apps like Pages, Mail, or Notes let you create eye-catching documents or messages. 
  • Accessibility: Bold font style can help people with dyslexia, low vision, or reading difficulties. 

Keeping this in mind, Apple offers text accessibility settings and app-specific font customization. 

Understanding Font Limitations in iOS

Before proceeding, it is worth noting that iPhone does not allow you to change the default font (such as menu or notification fonts) unless you have jailbroken the device. Apple uses its own font, San Francisco (SF Pro), for a consistent look across the iPhone.

However, there are several ways to adjust font size, weight, and style in settings or specific apps, and you can install custom fonts for use in supported apps like Pages, Keynote, Notes, or Mail.  

In the next section, I’ll share safe, non-jailbreak methods to customize your iPhone’s fonts. 

How to Change Font Size in iPhone Settings

The easiest way to tweak fonts on your iPhone is by adjusting the text size in the Settings app. This changes the font size system-wide, in most Apple apps (like Messages, Notes, and Mail), and some third-party apps that support Dynamic Type.

Here’s how to do it:

  1. Open the Settings app on your iPhone. 
  2. Tap Display & Brightness.
  3. Select Text Size. 
  4. Use the slider to make the text larger or smaller. You’ll see a preview of how the text will look.
  5. Tap Back to save your changes.

This method doesn’t change the font style (it stays as SF Pro), but it makes text easier to read. Changes apply instantly to supported apps. 

How to Make Text Bold and Adjust Display Contrast

For more control, you can make text bolder or use accessibility features:

Enable Bold Text:

  1. Go to Settings > Display & Brightness.
  2. Toggle on Bold Text.

Your iPhone will apply the changes instantly. This makes all system text (like app names and menus) bolder for better readability.

Use Accessibility Options:

  1. Open Settings and select Accessibility > Display & Text Size.
  2. Try these options:
    • Larger Text: Use the slider for even bigger font sizes than the standard Text Size setting.
    • Increase Contrast: Makes text and buttons stand out against backgrounds.

For specific apps, go to Settings > Accessibility > Per-App Settings and select an app to set custom font sizes for individual apps.

iOS 26 also introduced a new accessibility feature called Accessibility Reader to adjust font, spacing, and colors for any app or even physical text via Magnifier. These settings are great for users who need clearer text but don’t change the font family. 

How to Use Fonts in Notes, Pages, and Mail

Some Apple apps let you customize font style and typefaces, but only within the app itself. Here’s how: 

Customize Font Style in Notes App

In the Notes app, you can only change the text formatting to make it look organized.

  1. Open the Notes app and tap the pen icon to start a new note. 
  2. Tap the Aa button above the keyboard. 
  3. Choose from paragraph styles like Title, Heading, or Body. You can’t pick a new font family, but you can adjust the size and weight. 
  4. Tap the X icon and type your text. Changes apply only to that text.

Change Font Style in Apple Pages

You can create documents like reports, newsletters, flyers, cards, etc., with different fonts for more creative presentations.

  1. Launch the Pages app. Select Start Writing for a blank page or Choose a Template.  
  2. Tap the paintbrush icon at the top toolbar, then double-tap on the text to select it.
  3. Select the Font option to choose from available fonts or any custom fonts you’ve installed (more on that later). 
  4. Tap the info icon next to the font to select its typeface like Regular, Light, Semibold, Condensed, etc. 
  5. Now, tap < Text to get back and customize paragraph style, format, size, or text color as needed.

Tip: You can use the same steps on other iWork apps such as Keynote and Numbers. 

Change Font Style in Mail App (iOS 26+)

With iOS 26, you can customize your email text fonts for more personalization.  

  1. Open the Mail app and tap the pen icon to start writing an email.
  2. Tap the body text field and you will see a toolbar pop up above your keyboard.
  3. Select Aa from the toolbar.
  4. Tap Default Font dropdown in the menu and select Choose Font.
  5. Scroll through the built-in font list and choose a font.
  6. Now, you can write the email in that font.

By providing the native font library, Apple is opening its door to more customization. We hope to see more native apps include this feature.

How to Install Custom Fonts on iPhone

To use fonts beyond Apple’s defaults, you can install custom fonts for apps like Pages, Keynote, or third-party apps. Here are three ways to do it:

Method 1: Install Fonts from iPhone Settings

Apple has a default font library and multiple add-ons that you can download on your iPhone. These system fonts are available for use in the supported apps mentioned above.

  1. Go to Settings > General > Fonts.
  2. You will see System Fonts, where all the built-in fonts are listed.
  3. Select More fonts and tap the download icon next to a font to install it.  
  4. The font will be available in compatible apps.

Method 2: Use Font Installer Apps

Font installer apps make it easy to add new fonts in bundles. Popular apps include AnyFont, Font Diner, and others.

Let’s look at how to download and install custom fonts using the Font Diner app. The steps are similar for most font apps.

  1. Download and open the Font Diner app.
  2. Tap Activate next to the Silverware Font Set and tap Agree on the dialog box.
  3. Choose Install and tap Close.

Now, this font will be available in the supported apps. Font Diner allows you to download one free Silverware set of 23 fonts.

To get additional fonts, you must make an in-app annual purchase for other font sets.

Method 3: Use Configuration Profiles with iFont

Some websites or developers offer font configuration profiles to manually add fonts to your iPhone. Here’s how to do it using the iFont app:

  1. Open the iFont app and select Import Font.
  2. If you have downloaded a font file, select Import from Files. For this example, we’ll use Google Fonts.
  3. Scroll through the font library and tap Get to download it.
  4. Tap the X icon and swipe down to return to the home page.
  5. Tap Install next to the font and tap Continue to proceed.
  6. Tap Allow to install the configuration profile.

Now that you have downloaded the profile, you need to install it on your iPhone:

  1. Go to Settings > General > VPN & Device Management and select the profile.
  2. Tap Install at the top right corner and enter your passcode.
  3. Tap Install again in the dialog box.
  4. The font will now be available in supported apps.

Safety Tip: Only download profiles from reputable sources to avoid malware or any risks to your system.

How to Use Custom Fonts in Third-Party Apps

Many third-party apps, such as design tools and note-taking apps, support custom fonts. Here’s how to use them:

  1. Install a design app (e.g., Canva, Notion, or Procreate).
  2. Create a new project and look for the font menu in the text settings.
  3. Select your installed font from the list. You may see a “My Font” option.

How to Change Keyboard Fonts on iPhone

Some keyboard apps, like Fonts – AI Sticker or Keyboard Fonts, let you type with custom fonts in text-supported apps:

  1. Download a keyboard app from the App Store. 
  2. Go to Settings > General > Keyboard > Keyboards. 
  3. Tap Add New Keyboard and select the font keyboard.
  4. Select the keyboard again and toggle on Allow Full Access.
  5. Tap Allow to grant permission. 
  6. When typing in apps like Messages, tap the Globe icon to switch to the font keyboard and choose a style.

The first time, you may need to set up the keyboard from within the app.

Note: These keyboards only work in apps that allow custom keyboards, like Messages or WhatsApp, and may not support all fonts in every app.

Best Font Apps for iPhone in 2025

Here are some top-rated font apps for iPhone available on the App Store:

  • AnyFont: Offers a wide range of fonts and easy profile installation. Great for PowerPoint, Word, and Excel for iOS. 
  • Font Diner: Fun, creative fonts for design projects. Includes free and paid options. 
  • iFont App: Install fonts using TTF, OTF, or TTC format files. Also lets you access Google Fonts’ free font library.
  • Fonts – Install Fonts: A simple app with a mix of free and premium fonts, ideal for social media or notes. 
  • Font Generator: Popular for decorative fonts, perfect for messages or posts. 

Always check user reviews and ensure the app is updated for iOS 26 compatibility. 

Troubleshooting Font Installation Issues

If you run into problems, try these fixes: 

  • Font not showing in apps: Ensure the app supports custom fonts. Reinstall the font profile or restart your iPhone. 
  • Profile won’t install: Go to VPN & Device Management and check for errors. Download the profile again from a trusted source.
  • App crashes after font installation: Delete the font (Settings > General > Fonts) and try a different font or app.
  • Fonts look blurry: Some fonts may not be optimized for iOS. Choose high-quality fonts from reputable apps. 

If issues persist, contact the font app’s support team or Apple Support.

How to Manage and Remove Fonts on iPhone

To keep your iPhone running smoothly, manage your installed fonts:

  1. Go to Settings > General > Fonts. 
  2. Tap My Fonts to view all installed fonts. 
  3. Tap a font to see details like typefaces, copyright, and version.
  4. Tap the bin icon at the top and select Remove to delete it.

Regularly check for updates to font apps to ensure compatibility with the latest iOS version.

How to Revert to the Default Font

If you want to go back to Apple’s default font (SF Pro): 

  1. Remove custom font profiles: Go to VPN & Device Management, tap the font profile, and select Remove Profile. Enter your passcode and tap Remove to confirm.
  2. Reset text size: Go to Settings > Display & Brightness > Text Size and move the slider to the middle.
  3. Turn off Bold Text: In Display & Brightness, toggle off Bold Text.
  4. Restart your iPhone to apply all changes.

This will restore the default look of your iPhone’s text.

Final Thoughts

I hope this guide helped you customize your iPhone. While iOS doesn’t allow system-wide font changes, you can still resize and bold text, install custom fonts for creative or professional use, and type with stylish fonts using keyboard apps. With the introduction of Accessibility Reader, Apple is moving toward a more flexible and user-friendly typography experience.

Do you have a question? Feel free to ask in the comments below!

FAQs

Can I change the system-wide font on iPhone?

No. As of iOS 26, you can’t change the system-wide font without jailbreaking, which is risky and not recommended. You can adjust font size, weight, or use custom fonts in apps like Pages, Mail, or Notes.

What’s the best free font app for iPhone?

Fonts and Font Diner offer free fonts with optional in-app purchases. Check the App Store for the latest free options and read reviews to ensure they’re safe and compatible with the current iOS version.

Is it safe to install fonts using configuration profiles?

Yes, if you download profiles from trusted sources like reputable font apps or well-known developers. Avoid unknown websites to prevent malware or security issues.

Will changing fonts affect app performance?

Installing a few fonts won’t noticeably slow down your iPhone. However, too many font profiles or poorly designed fonts can use extra storage or cause minor lag in some apps. Manage fonts wisely to avoid issues.

itemListElement.text: Launch the Notes app from your home screen.

step.name: Select a paragraph style
step.text: Tap the Aa button just above the keyboard to see available text styles like Title, Heading, or Body.

itemListElement.text: Tap the Aa icon above your keyboard.

step.name: Access the formatting toolbar

keyPoints.title: Limitations of Changing System Fonts in iOS
keyPoints.explanation: iOS does not allow changing the default system-wide font, as Apple uses its own San Francisco font for consistency, but you can customize text size and style within supported apps.

keyPoints.title: Adjusting Font Size and Accessibility Features
keyPoints.explanation: You can easily change font size system-wide and toggle bold text or contrast in Settings, helping improve readability and accessibility without jailbreaking your device.

keyPoints.title: Using Fonts in Apple Apps like Notes, Pages, and Mail
keyPoints.explanation: Apple apps like Notes, Pages, and Mail allow font customization within the app, such as switching fonts in Pages or adjusting text styles in Mail, to enhance your document and message presentation.

keyPoints.title: Installing Custom Fonts Safely on iPhone
keyPoints.explanation: Custom fonts can be added via system font downloads in Settings, font installer apps like AnyFont, or configuration profiles from trusted sources, offering more style options for supported apps.

keyPoints.title: Managing and Reverting Fonts to Default
keyPoints.explanation: You can manage installed fonts through Settings or remove custom profiles to revert to the default SF Pro font, ensuring your device maintains optimal performance and appearance.

title.rendered: What Is iCloud Shared Photo Library and How Does It Work?

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • iCloud Shared Photo Library enables live collaboration between up to six people, syncing edits and additions across devices in real-time since iOS 16.1.
  • Simplifies event photo sharing by letting families or groups collect and manage all images in one space without constant AirDrop or message threads.
  • You can set it up from iPhone, iPad, or Mac by enabling iCloud Photos, selecting contributors, and choosing which photos to include or automate.
  • Invites are sent via Messages or Mail, and participants can choose what to share when they join – either all photos or ones from a date or people.
  • Shared mode replaces originals on all linked devices, so be cautious: deleting or editing a photo affects everyone, and privacy filters only go so far.

Apple’s iCloud Shared Photo Library has changed the way we share and store memories with our family and friends! Whether it’s a family vacation, group event, or just casual snapshots, this feature makes sharing photos and videos with your loved ones easy and collaborative.

In this guide, I’ll walk you through everything you need to know about iCloud Shared Photo Library, from setting it up to using and managing it on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

  • Why Use iCloud Shared Photo Library?

    • On Mac

    • On Mac

    • Manage Photos and Videos

      • On iPhone
      • On Mac
  • How to Remove Participants from Your Shared Library
    • On iPhone
    • On Mac
  • Delete Your Shared Photo Library
    • On iPhone
    • On Mac
  • How to Leave a Shared Library (Participant)
    • On iPhone
    • On Mac
  • Share Memories Quickly with iCloud Shared Library!

What Is iCloud Shared Photo Library?

iCloud Shared Photo Library is a feature introduced with iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, and macOS Ventura in late 2022. It allows up to six people, including the organizer, to share a single photo library in real time.

Unlike the standard iCloud Photo Library, which is private to one user, the Shared Photo Library lets participants add, edit, delete, and favorite photos and videos.

  • All media remains in full resolution with original metadata.
  • Everyone can see edits and changes instantly.
  • Shared content appears in Memories, Featured Photos, and the Photos widget just like personal content.
  • You can also take photos or videos and save them directly to the Shared Library.

The person who creates the Shared Library provides the iCloud storage, while other members can view and interact with the content without using their own iCloud space.

Important: If any participant uses an earlier iOS version, they won’t have access. Ensure all devices are updated.

Note Shared Albums and Shared Library are not the same. Shared Albums let you manually create albums shared with up to 100 people, but without full editing capabilities. Photos are compressed, and changes aren’t synced in real time.

If you haven’t tried Shared Albums, check out these guides:

  • How to Create Shared Albums on Your Mac
  • How to Use Shared Albums on iPhone and iPad

Why Use iCloud Shared Photo Library?

Here’s why iCloud Shared Photo Library is a game-changer:

  • Share photos and videos with up to five other people.
  • Changes sync instantly across all members’ devices.
  • Perfect for vacations, weddings, family events, and group hangouts where everyone can contribute.

How to Create an iCloud Shared Photo Library

Before starting, update your device and ensure you have enough iCloud storage or an active iCloud+ subscription. 

On iPhone and iPad 

  1. Open Settings, scroll down and tap Apps, select Photos and ensure iCloud Photos is toggled on.
  2. Tap Shared Library and then Get Started.
  3. Tap Add Participants and type an email or phone number in the recipients’ field or tap the plus icon (+) to select from your contacts (up to 5 people).
  4. Tap Add, then tap Next.
  5. Select which photos and videos to move to the Shared Library. Options include:
    • All My Photos and Videos: Share your entire photo library, excluding screenshots, deleted, or hidden photos and videos. 
    • Choose by People or Date: Add media sorted by specific people or dates from your library. You might want to do this for partners, for instance.  
    • Choose Manually: This lets you manually select what you share. It ensures that you only share the chosen pictures with the recipients. 
  6. Tap Next after picking an option. 
  7. In the following menu, you’ll see the people with whom you’re about to share your library. 
  8. Tap Next if you’re satisfied with the list.

If you’ve selected All My Photos and Videos:

  1. Select Preview Shared Library.
  2. Tap Continue at the top-right.

If you opted to choose by People or Date:

  1. You’ll get a prompt to identify the added contacts from your photos. Tap this prompt to sort your Shared Library by people. Ensure you select at least two people to continue. Tap Done at the top-right after identifying people.
  2. Next up is sorting pictures by date. Tap Start Date and set the date you want your Shared Library to span.
  3. Tap Next.
  4. Then select Preview Shared Library to view the pictures before sharing.
  5. Tap Continue at the top-right.

If you’re choosing pictures manually:

  1. Select the pictures you want to include in your Shared Library by tapping each.
  2. Tap Add at the top-right.
  3. Then tap Preview Shared Library.
  4. Tap Continue at the top-right.

After you have selected the photos, tap Invite via Messages to send an invite MMS to participants or tap Share Link to share the URL via social media. Choose to share your library Automatically or Manually via Bluetooth when participants are nearby. Finally, tap Done.

The Shared Library will now appear in the Photos app alongside your Personal Library. You can later add more participants from the Photos app > Collections tab > your account in the top-right corner > Shared Library > Manage > Add Participants.

Note You can only have one active Shared Photo Library at a time.

On Mac

  1. Open Photos app, go to Photos menu → Settings → iCloud tab.
  2. Ensure iCloud Photos is checked.
  3. Go to the Shared Library tab → Click Get Started.
  4. Click Add Participant, enter emails or phone numbers (up to 5 people).
  5. Click Add → Click Continue.
  6. Choose what to share (All, People/Date, or Manually) → Click Next.
  7. Select the photos and videos and click Add.
  8. Click Preview Shared Library and confirm by clicking Continue. Send invitations via Messages or a link.
  9. The Shared Library appears in the Photos app’s sidebar. You can view changes in the library from the Activity tab.
Tip If you start with a People album, you’ll get smart suggestions for content related to that person.

How to Join a Shared Library 

You need iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, macOS Ventura, or later. Kids under 13 can only join via Family Sharing.

On iPhone and iPad

  1. Tap the invitation link in Messages or Mail.
  2. Tap Accept & Continue and follow the prompts. 
  3. Select photos or videos from your Personal Library to add to the Shared Library. You can skip this step and add photos later. 
  4. Preview your selected photos, then confirm to join the library. 
  5. Open the Photos app. The Shared Library is accessible via the Library tab. 

On Mac 

  1. Click the invitation link → Click Get Started.
  2. Choose which photos or videos to contribute. You can skip this step. 
  3. Preview your selections, then confirm to join. The Shared Library appears in the Photos app’s sidebar. 

Once joined, you can add, edit, or delete content, and changes sync for all participants. 

Using iCloud Shared Photo Library on iPhone, iPad, and Mac

Once set up, managing and using the Shared Photo Library is intuitive, with options to organize content, save photos directly from your camera, and switch viewing modes. 

Manage Photos and Videos 

iCloud lets you manually add, edit, and delete photos and videos to your shared library. Here’s how:  

  • Add Photos: In the Photos app, select photos or videos from your Personal Library, tap the three-dot icon, and choose Move to Shared Library. All participants can add content. 
  • Edit Photos: Crop, apply filters, or adjust settings. Edits sync across all devices in real time. 
  • Delete Photos: Moves to Recently Deleted for 30 days. You’re notified if someone deletes your content.
  • Like and Comment: Add favorites, captions, or metadata visible to all.
  • Move Back to Personal Library: Tap the person icon → Select Move to Personal Library.

Save Camera Shots to Shared Library

Once you share an iCloud Library, you get to select where to save the output while making a video or taking a shot. For instance, if you choose Shared Library while taking a picture or making a video, the iPhone shares the output automatically. 

  1. Access Settings > Apps > Photos, and then select Shared Library.  
  2. Tap Sharing from Camera and ensure it is switched on. 
    • Choose Share Automatically if you want the Camera app to automatically add photos and videos to your Shared Library when you are near participants. Ensure all participants have Bluetooth enabled.  
    • To control when the Camera app adds photos, select Share Manually. 
  3. For automatic sharing photos taken at home to the Shared Library, toggle on Share When At Home. 

When you open your iPhone camera, look to the top left. You’ll see a double profile icon. Tap that icon to toggle between Shared and Personal Library for storage. 

Switch Viewing Modes

After creating a Shared Library, you can choose to show only the pictures you’ve shared, a personal library, or a mixture of both.

On iPhone

  • In the Photos app, tap Collections > your account in the top-right corner, and scroll down to Library View Options. Choose: 
    • Both Libraries: View Personal and Shared Library content together. 
    • Personal Library: View only your private photos. 
    • Shared Library: View only shared content. Shared photos have a person badge in the All Photos view. 

On Mac

  • In the Photos app, click the drop-down with the photo icon next to Library
    • Select Personal Library, Shared Library, or Both Libraries.

Note: Some features, like the People album, are only available in the Both Libraries view. 

How to Remove Participants from Your Shared Library 

As the library creator, you can remove participants at any time:

 On iPhone

  1. Go to Settings > Photos > Shared Library.
  2. Select the contact you want to remove, tap Remove from Shared Library and confirm your choice. 

On Mac

  1. Open Photos > Settings > Shared Library tab.
  2. Click the three-dot icon next to the participant’s name and select Remove. Select Remove from Shared Library.

Participants are notified, and if they’ve been in the library for more than 7 days, they can keep all shared content.

Delete Your Shared Photo Library 

To delete the entire Shared Library (creator only):

 On iPhone

  1. Go to Settings > Apps > Photos.
  2. Tap the Shared Library > Delete Shared Library. Confirm the action.

On Mac

  1. On Mac: In Photos > Settings > Shared Library and click Delete Shared Library.
  2. Choose which content you want to keep and select Delete Shared Library.

All participants receive a notification. If they were members for over seven days, they can download all iCloud photos and videos in their Personal Library. If less than seven days, they only get their contributed photos. Deleted photos go to the creator’s Recently Deleted folder for 30 days. 

How to Leave a Shared Library (Participant)

If you’re a participant, you can leave the Shared Library:

On iPhone 

  1. Go to Settings > Apps > Photos > Shared Library > Leave Shared Library.
  2. Choose to copy all content or only your contributions to your Personal Library. 

On Mac

  1. In Photos > Settings > Shared Library.
  2. Click Leave Shared Library and select your content preference. 

You’ll lose access. Others are notified. Your content remains unless you delete it before leaving.

Share Memories Quickly with iCloud Shared Library!

With iCloud Shared Photo Library, you can effortlessly share memories with people who matter most. It’s the perfect tool for organizing family photos, planning trips, or preserving moments with friends.

Have a question or issue? Drop it in the comments—I’m happy to help.

FAQs

Can Android users access iCloud Shared Library?

No. It works only on Apple devices with iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, or macOS Ventura or later. Android users can view shared items on iCloud.com but can’t contribute or edit. Use Shared Albums for basic sharing instead.

What happens when someone leaves the Shared Library?

They lose access. If they were members for more than seven days, they can download everything. Otherwise, they keep only their own content. Remaining participants are notified and the library continues.

mainEntity.name: Can Android users access iCloud Shared Library?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It works only on Apple devices with iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, or macOS Ventura or later. Android users can view shared items on iCloud.com but can't contribute or edit. Use Shared Albums for basic sharing instead.

mainEntity.name: What happens when someone leaves the Shared Library?

acceptedAnswer.text: They lose access. If they were members for more than seven days, they can download everything. Otherwise, they keep only their own content. Remaining participants are notified and the library continues.

keyPoints.title: Understanding iCloud Shared Photo Library
keyPoints.explanation: Introduced in late 2022, this feature lets up to six people share and collaboratively manage a single photo library in real-time.

keyPoints.title: Benefits of Using iCloud Shared Photo Library
keyPoints.explanation: It simplifies sharing memories with friends or family, allowing instant sync and collective editing for events like vacations and family gatherings.

keyPoints.title: Setting Up Your Shared Photo Library
keyPoints.explanation: Create a shared library on iPhone, iPad, or Mac by enabling iCloud Photos, selecting photos, and inviting others through the Photos app or device settings.

keyPoints.title: Joining a Shared Library Effortlessly
keyPoints.explanation: Participants receive an invitation via Messages or Mail to accept and select which content to contribute, enabling seamless collaboration.

keyPoints.title: Managing Shared Photos on Your Devices
keyPoints.explanation: After setup, you can organize, save new photos directly to the shared library, and view content modes that display shared, personal, or combined photos across Apple devices.

title.rendered: Jack Dorsey’s New Bitchat App Lets You Message Without the Internet

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • Jack Dorsey launches Bitchat for Apple devices using Bluetooth mesh to send encrypted messages without internet, covering iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Vision Pro.
  • Bluetooth mesh enables offline messaging by hopping messages between nearby devices, ideal for concerts, protests, or internet outages.
  • Bitchat prioritizes privacy and control with end-to-end encryption, no account needed, and a manual wipe button for emergencies.
  • User interface favors anonymity and simplicity with random handles, gesture-based chat access, and local-only discovery of nearby users.
  • Currently iOS-only with Android plans coming, Bitchat is free on the App Store and open-sourced on GitHub for public inspection.

Jack Dorsey, best known as Twitter’s co-founder and Block’s CEO, has quietly launched a new app called Bitchat. The messaging tool works without an internet connection, instead using a Bluetooth-based peer-to-peer mesh network. It’s currently available on the App Store for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Vision Pro.

Peer-to-Peer Messaging App That Works Without Internet

Bitchat doesn’t require users to exchange phone numbers or emails. Instead, it connects nearby devices using Bluetooth, forming a mesh network that allows encrypted messages to hop from one device to another. That setup enables communication in areas without cellular or Wi-Fi access, such as at crowded events or remote locations. The more people running the app, the broader the network coverage becomes.

The project comes out of “and Other Stuff,” an open-source initiative that Dorsey funds. According to its App Store listing, Bitchat offers a few key features:

The app’s description highlights a few key features:

  • Works without the internet: All communication happens over Bluetooth mesh.
  • Peer-assisted range: Messages travel by bouncing through nearby users running the app.
  • Focus on privacy: Messages are encrypted end-to-end.
  • Emergency wipe: A built-in Panic Mode erases all local app data with a triple tap.

The app automatically assigns each user a random @handle upon launch, which can be changed with a single tap. Users can swipe left or tap a top-right icon to browse active peers and initiate private chats.

App Now Live on App Store

Bitchat is currently available for free on the App Store, though it hasn’t rolled out in every region yet. The full source code is live on GitHub, opening the door for developers to inspect or build on the project. Dorsey acknowledged an early limitation: the current iOS build can’t connect to Android devices. A fix has already been submitted to Apple, and support for cross-platform messaging is expected soon.

Whether Bitchat evolves into a widely-used communication tool or remains a niche experiment, its launch points to ongoing interest in internet-free messaging. Especially in environments with unreliable connectivity or privacy concerns, mesh-based platforms like this hint at a broader rethink of how digital communication can function.

Would something like this be useful to you? Drop your thoughts in the comments.

mainEntity.name: Can Android users access iCloud Shared Library?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It works only on Apple devices with iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, or macOS Ventura or later. Android users can view shared items on iCloud.com but can't contribute or edit. Use Shared Albums for basic sharing instead.

mainEntity.name: What happens when someone leaves the Shared Library?

aioseo_meta_data.description: Jack Dorsey launches Bitchat, a peer-to-peer chat app for iPhone that works offline using Bluetooth mesh networking. No Wi-Fi, no phone number required.

keyPoints.title: Introduction of Bitchat by Jack Dorsey
keyPoints.explanation: Dorsey has launched Bitchat, a Bluetooth-based messaging app that operates without internet, available on Apple devices including iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Vision Pro.

keyPoints.title: How Bitchat Works Without Internet
keyPoints.explanation: The app uses Bluetooth to create a mesh network, enabling encrypted messages to hop between nearby devices, useful in areas without cellular or Wi-Fi access.

keyPoints.title: Key Features of Bitchat
keyPoints.explanation: Bitchat offers internet-free communication, peer-assisted message range, end-to-end encryption, and an emergency wipe feature for privacy and security.

keyPoints.title: User Experience and Interface
keyPoints.explanation: Users are assigned a random handle, can change it easily, and browse active peers or start private chats through intuitive gestures like swiping or tapping icons.

keyPoints.title: Availability and Future Support for Bitchat
keyPoints.explanation: Currently free on the App Store with source code on GitHub, the app is limited to iOS but plans are underway to add cross-platform messaging support, including Android.

title.rendered: Leaked Prototype Confirms Apple Considered iMac Logo Placement

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • Apple dropped the front logo on the 2021 iMac to highlight a cleaner look and embrace the minimalism trend seen across its latest hardware.
  • Early iMac prototypes included a front logo, showing Apple originally considered multiple branding placements before settling on the current bare-front design.
  • Minimalist design caters to younger aesthetics, with Apple favoring subtle branding and a more modern, decor-friendly profile for home setups.
  • Design decisions stem from extensive internal testing, with logo placement among the many tweaks that shift during prototype phases.
  • No front logo doesn’t mean it’s gone forever. Apple may revive visible branding on future iMacs, depending on design trends or market feedback.

Apple’s 2021 iMac redesign marked a major departure from previous generations, introducing vibrant color options, an ultra-slim chassis, and Apple Silicon for the first time in the lineup. But longtime users quickly noticed what wasn’t there: the familiar Apple logo that used to sit prominently on the front chin below the display.

Prototypes Reveal Logo Was Considered

While the absence of the front logo seemed like a bold aesthetic choice, it wasn’t a spontaneous one. A recent post by leaker Kosutami on X (formerly Twitter) shared a behind-the-scenes glimpse into early prototypes of the 24-inch iMac. One version reportedly included the Apple logo on the front, suggesting that Apple seriously weighed the decision before going in another direction.

In the final version, the logo was moved solely to the back, leaving the front panel minimal and logo-free. That design shift signals a clear intent by Apple to modernize the look while reducing brand clutter.

Design Shift Toward Visual Simplicity

The decision lines up with a broader trend in Apple’s hardware design: embracing cleaner lines and a minimalist presentation. The colorful finishes on the 2021 iMac already act as visual branding in themselves, perhaps making a front-facing logo feel redundant. It’s a calculated move that seems aimed at younger demographics, especially Gen Z buyers, who often favor understated design over overt branding.

How Apple Iterates Behind the Scenes

Kosutami’s leak underscores how Apple doesn’t land on a final design lightly. Each product reportedly goes through dozens of iterations, many of which never reach the public. While that level of control is nothing new, it’s rare to get a glimpse at these discarded variants.

It also leaves the door open for Apple to bring the logo back if design trends shift again or if a future iMac iteration calls for it. For now, the logo-free front appears to be a calculated statement.

Is a cleaner front worth the loss of the iconic logo? Or do you think the branding helped ground the iMac’s identity? Sound off in the comments below.

mainEntity.name: Can Android users access iCloud Shared Library?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It works only on Apple devices with iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, or macOS Ventura or later. Android users can view shared items on iCloud.com but can't contribute or edit. Use Shared Albums for basic sharing instead.

mainEntity.name: What happens when someone leaves the Shared Library?

acceptedAnswer.text: They lose access. If they were members for more than seven days, they can download everything. Otherwise, they keep only their own content. Remaining participants are notified and the library continues.

title.rendered: Remix Reels Like a Pro: How to Use Instagram’s Remix Feature Creatively

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • Instagram Remix lets you react or collaborate on Reels or posts with side-by-side or overlay formats using music, stickers, voiceovers, and more.
  • To remix a Reel, tap the three-dot menu and select Remix, then record or edit your response with Instagram’s built-in creative tools before posting.
  • You can also remix regular photo posts by using the same three-dot menu, enabling broader interaction beyond Reels.
  • Control who can remix your content by adjusting permissions in Settings or disabling reuse on individual posts and Reels.
  • Be mindful of remix etiquette and rights since remixing without permission or proper credit may lead to content takedowns or account issues.

Remixing a Reel on Instagram is a fun and simple way to add your voice to viral content. Whether you’re reacting to a trend, collaborating with another creator, or offering a fresh perspective, the Remix feature makes it possible, all from within the Instagram app. Best of all, you don’t need any advanced editing skills to get started.

Here’s how to remix Reels and posts on Instagram and manage your remixing preferences like a pro.

Table of Contents
  • What Is the Remix Feature on Instagram?
  • How to Remix a Reel on Instagram
  • How to Remix a Post on Instagram
  • How to Enable or Disable Remixing for Your Instagram Content
  • Final Thoughts: Ready to Remix?

What Is the Remix Feature on Instagram?

Instagram’s Remix feature is its answer to TikTok’s popular Duet option. It lets you create a new Reel that appears side-by-side, beneath, or overlaid on another creator’s video. You can also customize it with:

  • Music
  • Text
  • Stickers
  • Filters
  • Voiceovers

This tool is perfect for:

  • Reacting to videos
  • Launching or joining challenges
  • Collaborating with other creators
  • Adding commentary or creative takes

How to Remix a Reel on Instagram

If the original Reel has remixing enabled, you can easily create your version—whether you’re using an iPhone or Android. Here’s how:

  1. Open Instagram and tap the Reels tab at the bottom.
  2. Scroll through the Reels until you find the one you want to remix.
  3. Tap the three-dot (More Options) button in the bottom right corner of the Reel.
  4. Tap the Remix button in the pop-up menu.

  5. Use the tools in the bottom toolbar to:
    • Add music
    • Apply stickers and filters
    • Add text or a voiceover
  6. To adjust how your remix appears:
    • Tap the Camera icon
    • Tap Layout and choose side-by-side or picture-in-picture

  7. Record a new clip using the Capture button or upload from your Photo Library.
  8. Once done, tap Next.
  9. Add music, text, stickers, filters, or voiceovers just like you would with any Reel.
  10. Once you’re happy, tap Next, write a caption, and share it with your followers.

That’s it! You’ve just remixed your first Instagram Reel.

Related: How to Download Instagram Reels on iPhone

How to Remix a Post on Instagram

You can also remix regular posts (if remixing is enabled for them):

  1. Tap the three–dot menu at the top-right corner of the post.
  2. Select Remix.
  3. Add effects, record or upload your clip, and share it.

You’ll have access to the same creative tools as with Reel remixes.

How to Enable or Disable Remixing for Your Instagram Content

While remixing others’ content can be exciting, you might not want people to remix yours. Thankfully, Instagram gives you full control.

Disable Remixing for a Specific Reel or Post:

  1. Open Instagram and head to your profile.
  2. Open any Reel or post.
  3. Tap the three-dot button, then select the Turn Off Reuse.
  4. Tap Turn off to confirm.

These steps will disable remixing for the specific Reel but not for new or other existing Reels and posts.

To turn off remixing across the board on all your Reels and posts, follow these steps:

  1. Head to your Instagram profile and tap the Hamburger icon at the top right corner.
  2. Scroll down to the “How others can interact with you” section and select the “Sharing and reuse” option under it.
  3. Here, toggle off Reels and Posts under the “Allow other people to create with and reuse your content” section.

Once disabled, no one can remix any of your content going forward.

Final Thoughts: Ready to Remix?

Instagram’s Remix feature offers a powerful way to connect with trends, express your creativity, and collaborate with others. Whether you’re reacting, responding, or creating new challenges, the Remix tool helps you engage with your audience in dynamic ways.

Important Always avoid using someone else’s content for commercial purposes without their permission. Doing so can result in your account being flagged or restricted.

Have you tried remixing a Reel yet? Drop your experience in the comments below!

  • How to Turn Off Active Status on Instagram & Stay Hidden
  • Instagram Blend: Share a personalized reels feed with friends
  • Link Reels on Instagram: Everything You Need to Know

mainEntity.name: Are UDID and serial number similar on iPhone?

acceptedAnswer.text: UDID and serial number are two distinct things. The UDID is a unique 40-character alphanumeric code used by developers to identify an individual iPhone or iPad. The serial number, on the other hand, is a distinct string of numbers and letters that identifies a specific iPhone model.

mainEntity.name: Can I change the system-wide font on iPhone?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. As of iOS 26, you can't change the system-wide font without jailbreaking, which is risky and not recommended. You can adjust font size, weight, or use custom fonts in apps like Pages, Mail, or Notes.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to install fonts using configuration profiles?

mainEntity.name: Will changing fonts affect app performance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Installing a few fonts won't noticeably slow down your iPhone. However, too many font profiles or poorly designed fonts can use extra storage or cause minor lag in some apps. Manage fonts wisely to avoid issues.

mainEntity.name: Can Android users access iCloud Shared Library?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It works only on Apple devices with iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, or macOS Ventura or later. Android users can view shared items on iCloud.com but can't contribute or edit. Use Shared Albums for basic sharing instead.

mainEntity.name: What happens when someone leaves the Shared Library?

acceptedAnswer.text: They lose access. If they were members for more than seven days, they can download everything. Otherwise, they keep only their own content. Remaining participants are notified and the library continues.

@graph.name: How to Remix a Reel on Instagram
@graph.description: Create your own version of an Instagram Reel by remixing with filters, voiceovers, and layout tools to personalize and share your content.

step.name: Open the Reels tab
step.text: Open Instagram and tap the Reels tab at the bottom of the screen.

itemListElement.text: Launch Instagram and tap the Reels icon at the bottom.

step.name: Select the Reel to remix
step.text: Scroll until you find a Reel you want to remix, then tap the three-dot button in the bottom right corner.

itemListElement.text: Browse through Reels and find one you want to remix.
Tap the three-dot More Options button.

step.name: Tap Remix
step.text: Tap the Remix option from the pop-up menu to begin creating your remix.

itemListElement.text: Tap Remix in the pop-up menu.

step.name: Customize your remix
step.text: Use the bottom toolbar to add music, text, stickers, or a voiceover. Tap the Camera icon to adjust layout using side-by-side or picture-in-picture modes.

itemListElement.text: Use tools at the bottom to add music, text, or stickers.
Tap the Camera icon and choose your layout style.

step.name: Record or upload your clip
step.text: Press the Capture button to record your remix or upload a video from your photo library.

itemListElement.text: Tap the Capture button to record or select a clip to upload.

step.name: Finalize and share your remix
step.text: Once you're done editing, tap Next, add a caption, and share your remix with followers.

itemListElement.text: Tap Next to preview your remix.
Add a caption and tap Share to post it.

@graph.name: How to Remix a Post on Instagram
@graph.description: Quickly remix any Instagram post by adding your own video, filters, and effects to share a creative response.

step.name: Access the post
step.text: Tap the three-dot menu in the top-right corner of the Instagram post you want to remix.

itemListElement.text: Open the post and tap the three-dot menu in the top-right corner.

step.name: Select Remix
step.text: Tap the Remix option from the menu that appears.

itemListElement.text: Choose Remix from the options listed.

step.name: Create and share your remix
step.text: Add effects, record or upload your video, and then share your remix like a regular post.

itemListElement.text: Apply filters or effects and record your video or upload one.
Tap Share to post your remix.

keyPoints.title: What Is the Remix Feature on Instagram?
keyPoints.explanation: Instagram's Remix feature allows users to create side-by-side, overlaid, or beneath videos similar to TikTok's Duet, enabling reactions, collaborations, and creative commentary with added tools like music, stickers, and filters.

keyPoints.title: How to Remix a Reel on Instagram
keyPoints.explanation: To remix a Reel, open the Reel, tap the three-dot menu, select Remix, and then use the editing tools to add music, effects, or record a new clip before sharing your remix.

keyPoints.title: How to Remix a Post on Instagram
keyPoints.explanation: Remixing a post involves tapping the three-dot menu on a post, choosing Remix, and then using available creative tools to add effects, record or upload a clip, and share it.

keyPoints.title: How to Enable or Disable Remixing for Your Instagram Content
keyPoints.explanation: You can control remix permissions by turning off reuse for specific Reels or posts, or disable remixing entirely from your profile settings under 'Sharing and reuse' to prevent others from remixing your content.

keyPoints.title: Final Thoughts: Ready to Remix?
keyPoints.explanation: The Remix feature is a versatile tool for engaging with trends and collaborating, but always respect content rights to avoid issues with misuse or account restrictions.

title.rendered: How to Set Any Song as iPhone Ringtone Without iTunes or PC

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • Personalized ringtones reflect your style and make it easier to identify calls or assign custom tones to contacts on your iPhone.
  • iOS 26 lets you set ringtones directly from the Files app without needing a Mac, iTunes, or third-party tools.
  • DRM-free audio files are required and must be under 30 seconds to work as ringtones; Apple Music tracks won’t work due to DRM.
  • GarageBand offers full control for trimming and exporting custom ringtones, either directly on iPhone or via Mac.
  • Be cautious with third-party ringtone apps as they may include ads, upsells, or require manual export steps to complete the process.

Ever picked up your iPhone only to realize it was someone else’s ringing with the same default tone? If you’re ready to stand out, it’s time to give your iPhone a personal touch.

The best part? You can use your favorite song as a ringtone—no iTunes, no computer required. In this guide, I’ll show you multiple methods to create and set a custom ringtone using your iPhone, Mac, or apps.

Table of Contents
  • Why Set a Custom Ringtone on iPhone?
  • What You Need Before You Start
  • Method 1: Set Custom Ringtone on iOS 26 (No App or Computer Required)
  • Method 2: Use GarageBand (iOS 18 or earlier)
  • Method 3: Create Ringtones on Mac Using Apple Music
  • Method 4: Use Third-Party Ringtone Maker Apps
  • Assign a Custom Ringtone to a Contact
  • Video: How to Set Any Song as Ringtone on iPhone

Why Set a Custom Ringtone on iPhone?

Setting a custom ringtone is more than fun—it’s practical:

  • Personal expression: Showcase your music taste.
  • Easy recognition: Identify your phone instantly in noisy areas.
  • Custom caller ID: Assign unique tones to specific contacts.
  • Mood booster: Let your ringtone uplift your mood.
  • Break the monotony: Ditch the default iPhone tone.
  • Professional vibe: Use a subtle tone for business settings.

What You Need Before You Start

Make sure you have:

  • A DRM-free audio file (MP3, AAC, or M4R)
  • File saved in the Files or Music app
  • Audio duration of 30 seconds or less
  • GarageBand or a ringtone maker app (for iOS 18 and below)
  • Enough iPhone storage

Note: Apple Music tracks are DRM-protected and can’t be used.

Method 1: Set Custom Ringtone on iOS 26 (No App or Computer Required)

iOS 26 makes it incredibly easy to use your song as a ringtone—no GarageBand or Mac needed.

Steps:

  1. Open the Files app and go to the folder where your audio file is stored.
  2. If the file exceeds 30 seconds, trim it using an audio editor.
  3. Tap the audio file to open it.
  4. Tap the Share button (bottom-right corner in Files or three-dots in Voice Memos).
  5. Scroll through the Share Sheet and select “Use as Ringtone.” If not visible, tap More to find it.
  6. The audio file will be added to the ringtone list and automatically set as your default ringtone.

To confirm or change it, go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Ringtone.

Tip: If “Use as Ringtone” doesn’t appear, quit and reopen the Files app, and check the file format.

Developer Beta Note: iOS 26 is in beta—don’t install it on your main device due to possible bugs or app issues.

If your iPhone is running iOS 18 or earlier, follow the methods below using GarageBand or Mac.

Method 2: Use GarageBand (iOS 18 or earlier)

If you’re on iOS 18 or below, use GarageBand:

  1. Launch the GarageBand app on your iPhone.
  2. Swipe and find Audio Recorder from the options, and tap Voice (mic icon). You can also use a Keyboard or Drummer for this purpose.

  3. Here, tap View (brick wall-like icon) to enter the editing section.

  4. Tap the Loop icon. You’ll see three subheadings here – Apple Loops, Files, and Music.
    Since my ringtone is saved in files, I will be using that tab.

  5. Look for the song you want; tap and hold it for a few seconds to import the file. If you can’t see the song, tap Browse items from the Files app to find it.

  6. To edit the song, drag the long vertical bar to the desired starting point of your custom ringtone. Then, use the play button to achieve the perfect starting point of your tone.
  7. Once done, double-tap the song and select Split.

  8. Drag the Scissor icon down to cut/divide the song at your chosen point.
  9. Delete the unusable part of the song by tapping it twice and then choosing Delete.

  10. Now, select the down arrow icon from the top-left corner and tap My Songs.

  11. Tap and hold the project and select Share from the list.
  12. Select Ringtone, then continue, name the song as per your choice, and tap Export.

  13. Once the process completes, tap Use sound as… to set it as a ringtone directly or OK to do it manually.

  14. If you have selected Use sound as…, you will see options to set the ringtone as Standard Ringtone. To change the ringtone for a specific caller, select Assign to contact.

Note While exporting, the iPhone automatically trims the ringtone at 30 seconds. If you want to set an endpoint somewhere before 30 seconds, repeat steps 6 to 9.

If you find the GarageBand method daunting, don’t worry. You can make a custom ringtone using Apple Music. Yes, you heard it right! Let me show you.

Method 3: Create Ringtones on Mac Using Apple Music

Before you start, ensure you have the DRM-free song file saved locally on your Mac.

Steps to follow:

  1. Launch Apple Music on your Mac.
  2. Select Songs from the left pane and locate the track.
    If you can’t find it, drag and drop the song file to the Music app window.
  3. Play the song and move your cursor to the playing tile at the top.
  4. Note the time stamp where you want your ringtone to start and end. The time gap should be 40 seconds max.

  5. Now, right-click on the track and select Get Info from the context menu.

  6. It will pop up a new window with song details. Move to the Options tab.
  7. Enter the Start and Stop time stamp you noted and click OK.

  8. Next, select the track and click File on the menu bar.
  9. Select the Convert option and choose Create AAC Version.
    If you only have the Create MP3 version option, click it.

  10. You will see a new track with the time length you set under the original track. Right-click on the new track and select Show in Finder.

  11. It will redirect you to Finder. The track will have the same name as the original and a .m4a extension. Right-click on the track and select Rename.

  12. Write .m4r in the extension and hit the Enter key. M4R is a file format specifically designed for iPhone ringtones.
  13. Select the Use .m4r option to confirm it.

Your custom iPhone ringtone is ready! If you have the ringtone file in .mp3 format, you can use an online converter to create the .m4r file. Once done, follow the steps below to set the song as a ringtone on your iPhone.

  1. Take a USB cable and connect your Mac to your iPhone. Click Trust on your Mac and enter your iPhone passcode if prompted.
  2. Navigate to the open Finder window. Click File on the menu bar and select New Finder Window. Ensure the previous window with the track is not closed.

  3. Click your iPhone name from the left sidebar of the new Finder window. It will show your iPhone details.
  4. Now, drag and drop the .m4r file to the new Finder window. You will see a green plus icon, indicating the song file will be added to your iPhone.

  5. You may now unplug your iPhone from your Mac.
  6. Next, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and select Sounds & Haptics.
  7. Tap on the Ringtone option.
  8. Here, you can see the ringtone you just made. Select it.

That’s it! You have successfully changed your ringtone to your favorite song.

Note

If you have a Windows PC, you can use the iTunes app. Start by cutting the songs to form a 40-second track. The next thing to do is use iTunes to convert it to an AAC format. Afterward, drag and drop the AAC file into any folder. Consequently, this will result in a .m4r extension. Finally, connect your PC to your iPhone and click on the iPhone icon in iTunes. Go to Tones and drop the .m4r file there.

Method 4: Use Third-Party Ringtone Maker Apps

I know the above-mentioned methods are a bit lengthy and time-consuming. If you are struggling with Apple’s built-in methods or don’t have a computer, several third-party apps are available to simplify the process. Such apps offer advanced features and flexibility.

Here are some popular ringtone apps for iPhone you can use:

  • Garage Ringtones for iPhone: This app enables you to create ringtones using songs and videos. There is an easy-to-use platform for cutting songs and setting ringtones.
  • RingTune: You can browse through popular ringtones from the RingTune library or songs saved on your iPhone. Moreover, the app recommends ringtones that match your interests.
  • Ringtones: for iPhone: The app can be used to easily modify, trim and produce unique ringtones. You can also record audio for your ringtone.
  • Ringtones Maker – the ring app: If you want advanced music editing, go for this app. It lets you precisely cut the song and add fade-in filters to the ringtone.

You may choose any of the apps to create custom ringtones for your iPhone. The process is similar: open the app, import your song file, cut it to make a 40-second track, and set it as a ringtone. Nevertheless, specific steps may differ depending on the app you select. Always follow the app’s guidelines and tutorials for optimal use.

You may be wondering whether third-party apps are worth it. Let’s examine some pros and cons of iPhone ringtone apps.

Pros

  • Easy to use
  • Pre-built ringtone libraries
  • Editing tools and voice recording
  • Frequent updates with new sounds

Cons

  • In-app purchases or ads
  • Potential privacy risks if permissions are misused
  • Not all apps are compatible with older iPhones

Assign a Custom Ringtone to a Contact

Want a specific ringtone for someone special?

Steps:

  1. Launch the Contacts app on your iPhone.
  2. Scroll through and select the contact for whom you want to set a custom ringtone.
  3. Tap the Edit button located in the upper right corner.
  4. Scroll down until you see the Ringtone option. Select it to open the ringtone selection menu.

  5. You will see a list of available ringtones, including the ones you added. Choose the desired ringtone. A checkmark will appear next to your choice.
  6. Finally, tap Done in the upper right corner to save your choice. Then, hit Done again to exit the contact editing screen.

Now, that person has a unique ringtone just for them!

Video: How to Set Any Song as Ringtone on iPhone

Signing off…

Now that you know how to set any song as your iPhone ringtone, there’s no excuse to settle for the default. Whether you’re making your iPhone more fun, unique, or professional, a custom ringtone adds that personal touch.

Still have questions? Drop them in the comments below—we’re happy to help.

Read more:

  • How to make your iPhone ring even when it’s on silent
  • Way to fix iPhone not ringing when locked
  • No sound during calls on iPhone? 12 Ways to fix it!

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It works only on Apple devices with iOS 16.1, iPadOS 16.1, or macOS Ventura or later. Android users can view shared items on iCloud.com but can't contribute or edit. Use Shared Albums for basic sharing instead.

mainEntity.name: What happens when someone leaves the Shared Library?

keyPoints.explanation: Custom ringtones let you showcase your music taste, recognize calls easily, assign specific tones to contacts, and add a fun or professional touch to your device.

keyPoints.title: Requirements for Creating Ringtones
keyPoints.explanation: You'll need DRM-free audio files of 30 seconds or less, saved in Files or Music app, and compatible apps like GarageBand or ringtone makers, noting that Apple Music tracks are DRM-protected.

keyPoints.title: Setting Ringtones on iOS 26 Without Apps
keyPoints.explanation: You can directly use the Files app to trim and set a song as a ringtone in iOS 26, simplifying the process without needing a computer or extra apps.

keyPoints.title: Creating Ringtones Using GarageBand or Mac
keyPoints.explanation: GarageBand for iOS or Apple Music on Mac allows precise editing, trimming, and exporting of songs as .m4r files, which can then be transferred to the iPhone as custom ringtones.

keyPoints.title: Using Third-Party Apps for Ringtone Creation
keyPoints.explanation: Third-party apps offer easier, flexible options for creating and editing ringtones, often with additional features like libraries, voice recording, and advanced editing tools, making the process quicker and more customizable.

title.rendered: How to Downgrade macOS 26 Tahoe Beta to macOS Sequoia Without Losing Your Data

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • macOS 26 Tahoe beta can break apps and workflows due to bugs, crashes, and system instability not ready for daily use.
  • Back up before downgrading using Time Machine, iCloud, or manual copies to avoid permanent data loss when reinstalling macOS Sequoia.
  • Choose a downgrade method that fits your setup: Time Machine for easiest recovery, bootable USB for clean install, or Internet Recovery if unprepared.
  • Time Machine restores both system and files if you backed up before installing macOS 26, making it the safest rollback option.
  • Clean installs require a bootable USB drive and Terminal commands, better suited for advanced users doing a full wipe and reinstall.

Apple’s macOS 26 Tahoe introduces exciting features like the Liquid Glass UI, the native Phone app, Live Activities on desktop, improved Spotlight search, and more. However, being early beta software, it’s also prone to bugs, app crashes, performance lags, and compatibility issues. If your Mac feels sluggish or unstable, downgrading to the reliable macOS 15 Sequoia could be your best bet.

In this guide, I’ll walk you through multiple methods to remove macOS 26 Tahoe Beta and safely revert to macOS Sequoia—without losing your apps, settings, or precious files.

Why You Might Want to Downgrade

macOS beta versions are meant for developers and early adopters. While they offer a sneak peek into future features, they also come with risks:

  • Apps may crash or behave unpredictably.
  • Features like the new Games app or Continuity may not function properly.
  • Your Mac could overheat or perform sluggishly due to unoptimized code.
  • Constant beta updates can disrupt daily workflow.
  • Some third-party apps or external hardware might not be compatible yet.

By downgrading, you regain stability—especially crucial if you use your Mac for professional tasks or schoolwork.

What to Do Before Removing macOS 26 Beta

Before downgrading, take these essential steps to avoid data loss and prep your Mac.

1. Remove the Beta Profile

To stop receiving macOS 26 beta updates:

  1. Open System Settings from the Apple menu () in the top-left corner. 
  2. Go to General > Software Update. 
  3. Click the info (i) icon next to Beta Updates. 
  4. Now, click the dropdown next to Beta Updates. 
  5. Select Off from the list of options. 
  6. Confirm by clicking Done and restart your Mac if prompted. 

This ensures your Mac will only receive stable macOS Sequoia updates after the downgrade.

2. Take a Full Backup

Since downgrading erases your Mac’s drive, backing up your data is crucial. Choose one or more of the following:

Time Machine Backup

  1. Connect an external drive (at least twice your Mac’s storage, e.g., 1TB for a 500GB Mac). 
  2. Go to System Settings > General > Time Machine. 
  3. Click Add Backup Disk, select your external drive, and follow the prompts. 

  4. Wait for the backup to complete (this may take hours depending on data size). 

iCloud Backup

  1. Go to System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud. 
  2. Enable iCloud Drive and ensure Desktop & Documents Folders are toggled on.  
  3. Also, click Apps syncing to iCloud Drive and toggle on the apps. 

  4. Check storage availability (you may need to purchase more iCloud space). 

Manual Backup

  1. Copy important files (documents, photos, videos) to an external drive or cloud service like Google Drive or Dropbox. 
  2. Double-check that all critical data is saved. 

Tip: Back up any files created after upgrading to macOS 26 separately. Time Machine backups made on macOS 26 can’t be restored to Sequoia.

How to Downgrade From macOS 26 Tahoe to macOS Sequoia

You’ll need to erase your Mac’s disk and reinstall macOS Sequoia using one of the following three methods:

Quick Overview of the Methods 

Method 1: Use Time Machine Backup

If you created a Time Machine backup before installing macOS 26 Beta, this method is the most straightforward.

Time Estimate: 1–3 hours, depending on backup size and drive speed. 

Steps:

  1. Plug in the external drive that contains your Time Machine backup. 
  2. Shut down your Mac. Press and hold the power button until “Loading startup options” appears.  
  3. Click Options > Continue. Your Mac will enter Recovery mode. 
  4. Select your administrative account and enter your Mac password. 
  5. In the macOS Utilities menu, select Restore from Time Machine Backup and click Continue. 
  6. Choose your Time Machine backup drive. 
  7. Select the most recent backup from when your Mac ran macOS Sequoia. 
  8. Follow the on-screen instructions to erase the drive and restore your data, apps, and settings. 

Your Mac will restart with macOS Sequoia, and your previous settings, apps, and files will remain intact.

Method 2: Use Internet Recovery

Internet Recovery reinstalls the macOS version your Mac had before upgrading. First, you need to factory reset your Mac using Disk Utility.  

Time Estimate: 3–4 hours for erasing the disk, downloading macOS, and setting up Mac. 

Steps:

  1. Enter Recovery mode using the steps above. 
  2. In the macOS Utilities menu, select Disk Utility > Continue.  
  3. Choose Macintosh HD (your main drive) and click Erase.  
  4. Set the format to APFS (or Mac OS Extended (Journaled) for older Macs) and select the Erase button.  
  5. Enter your Apple ID if asked and click Erase Mac and Restart. 

After the Mac has restarted, follow the on-screen prompts. Next, join a Wi-Fi network and select Exit to Recovery Utilities to quit Disk Utility. Now, you can revert from macOS Tahoe beta to macOS Sequoia. 

  1. Back in the macOS Utilities menu, select Reinstall macOS Sequoia and click Continue. 
  2. Enter your Mac password if prompted and select Macintosh HD to install the macOS. 
  3. Follow the prompts to download and install the macOS version. 
  4. Your Mac will restart and show the setup assistant. Follow the instructions to restore your data. 
  5. During setup, choose Transfer from a Time Machine Backup or manually copy files from your external drive or iCloud.  

Method 3: Use a Bootable macOS Sequoia Installer

For those who want complete control over the downgrade, this method is ideal.

Time Estimate: 1–2 hours for setup and installation, plus time for data restoration.

Steps to Create Installer: 

  1. Open the App Store and search for macOS Sequoia. 
  2. Click View > Get to save the installer to your Applications folder. 
  3. Connect a USB drive (minimum 32GB) and rename it for easy identification (e.g. MyVolume). 
  4. Open Disk Utility via Spotlight, select the USB drive, and click Erase. 
  5. Set the format to APFS and click Erase. 
  6. Open the Terminal and enter sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Sequoia.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume 
  7. Enter your admin password and wait until you see the message: “Media now available at…” (10–30 minutes). 

Now, you can use this USB drive to boot macOS Sequoia on your Mac. Reset your Mac using the steps above then: 

  1. Quit Disk Utility and connect to a Wi-Fi network. Enter your Apple ID if prompted. 
  2. Click the Apple logo at the top and select Restart.  
  3. Connect the USB drive to your Mac. 
  4. Press and hold the power button until “Loading startup options” appears. Select the USB drive and click Continue. 
  5. Select Install macOS Sequoia. 
  6. Follow the prompts to install Sequoia.  

Now, you can restore your Mac from backup or external drive. 

Post-Downgrade Checklist

Once you’re back on macOS Sequoia:

  • If you used the Time Machine method, your files, apps, and settings should already be restored. For manual backups, copy files from your external drive or iCloud to their original locations. 
  • Some apps (e.g., Adobe, Microsoft Office) may require re-entering licenses or signing in again. 
  • Verify Wi-Fi, iCloud, and other system settings are correct. 
  • Go to System Settings > General > Software Update to install the latest Sequoia patches. 

What to Do If Sequoia Doesn’t Download

If you face issues downloading or installing:

  • Make sure your Mac is Sequoia-compatible (most Apple Silicon and newer Intel Macs are). 
  • Use a reliable, high-speed connection. If necessary, restart your router. 
  • Free up at least 25–50 GB of storage space on your Mac to ensure a smooth installation. 
  • If the App Store fails, download the Sequoia installer from Apple’s support website or use Internet Recovery. 
  • For professional guidance, contact Apple Support.  

How to Stop Getting macOS Beta Updates

To avoid beta versions in the future:

  1. Go to System Settings > General > Software Update and confirm Beta Updates is set to Off. 
  2. Click the i button next to Automatic Updates. 
  3. Toggle off Download new updates when available and Install macOS updates. 

Now, you can manually install only stable macOS versions like Sequoia.

Enjoy macOS Sequoia’s Stability

Downgrading from macOS 26 Tahoe Beta to macOS Sequoia isn’t complicated if you follow the right steps. Just remember to back up first, pick the method that suits your situation, and take your time during restoration.

By switching back, you regain speed, reliability, and compatibility—without losing your valuable data or productivity.

  • How to downgrade macOS 27 Beta to macOS Tahoe

step.name: Connect your external drive
step.text: Plug in an external drive that has at least twice the storage of your Mac, for example, a 1TB drive for a 500GB Mac.

itemListElement.text: Use a USB, Thunderbolt, or network-attached external drive.
Ensure it has at least twice the storage space of your Mac.

step.name: Set up Time Machine
step.text: Go to System Settings, click General, then Time Machine. Add your external drive and follow the prompts to start the backup.

itemListElement.text: Click on System Settings from the Apple menu.
Navigate to General, then choose Time Machine.
Click Add Backup Disk and select your connected external drive.
Follow the on-screen prompts to initiate the backup process.

@graph.name: How to Take a Full Backup using iCloud Backup
@graph.description: Learn how to create a full backup of your Mac using iCloud Backup to keep your files, apps, and documents safe and accessible across devices.

step.name: Open iCloud Settings
step.text: Go to System Settings and click on your Apple ID at the top to open iCloud settings.

itemListElement.text: Click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen.
Select System Settings from the dropdown menu.
Click your name at the top of the sidebar to access your Apple ID and iCloud settings.

step.name: Enable iCloud Drive and Sync Apps
step.text: Make sure iCloud Drive is turned on and that your Desktop & Documents folders are being synced, along with the apps you want backed up.

itemListElement.text: Turn on iCloud Drive if it isn’t already enabled.
Toggle on Desktop & Documents Folders to include them in the backup.
Click the 'Apps syncing to iCloud Drive' section and turn on any apps you want to back up.

step.name: Check iCloud Storage
step.text: Ensure you have enough iCloud storage for your backup. If needed, consider upgrading your storage plan.

itemListElement.text: Review your current iCloud storage usage in the iCloud settings.
Click 'Manage Storage' to see details and upgrade if necessary.

keyPoints.title: Methods for Downgrading

title.rendered: iPhone 17 Pro Prototype Spotted in the Wild? Here’s What We Know

content.rendered:
Key Takeaways:

  • iPhone 17 Pro prototype may have been spotted in LA with leaked photos showing a man holding a mystery device in a bulky disguise case.
  • Rectangular camera bar and LiDAR hint at design changes despite Apple’s efforts to obscure details with casing and security guards shielding the device.
  • Rumored upgrades include a 48MP telephoto lens and A19 Pro chip plus a wider camera bar, vapor chamber cooling, and anti-reflective glass coating.
  • Leaked prototype sightings are rare this early, making this photo unusual and heightening interest in what could be a major iPhone redesign.
  • Treat early leaks with skepticism since prototype hardware often differs from final units and may never reflect the actual shipping product.

Just ahead of Apple’s expected September keynote, a new round of grainy photos is stirring speculation online. This time, allegedly shows an early version of the iPhone 17 Pro out in the wild.

Alleged iPhone 17 Pro Prototype Surfaces in Los Angeles

Two low-quality images shared by X user @Skyfops appear to capture a man holding what looks like a prototype iPhone, photographed somewhere in Los Angeles. One device resembles an iPhone 16 Pro with its Apple logo obscured. The other, larger, chunkier, and wrapped in a thick black case, is rumored to be a disguised iPhone 17 Pro test unit.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reposted the photos with the caption, “This looks legit,” though it’s not entirely clear whether he meant that seriously or sarcastically. Given Gurman’s reputation and the lack of context, it’s left many reading between the lines.

The bulky case seems intentionally designed to hide the phone’s final design. Still, some elements peek through: a set of circular openings for the LED flash and LiDAR scanner appear on the right side, aligning with prior leaks that suggest the iPhone 17 Pro will feature a wide, rectangular camera bar stretching across the back.

A second man, assumed to be part of Apple’s internal security team, was spotted nearby, attempting to shield the phone from view whenever it was in use. A similar sighting was reported earlier this summer in San Francisco’s Union Square, where someone was seen handling a similarly encased device.

What the Rumors Point To

Leaked schematics and supply chain chatter have already painted a fairly consistent picture of what to expect from the iPhone 17 Pro. These latest sightings, while unclear, seem to reinforce several of those rumored design shifts:

  • A rectangular camera bar stretching across the width, with vertically stacked LED flash and LiDAR components on the right.
  • A repositioned Apple logo, likely shifted lower to accommodate the new camera alignment.
  • An upgraded 48MP telephoto lens for sharper zoom images.
  • Anti-reflective screen coating aimed at cutting glare outdoors.
  • Apple’s upcoming A19 Pro chip is paired with 12GB of RAM on the Pro models.
  • A thinner chassis, made possible by the revamped camera bump.
  • Vapor chamber cooling helps regulate device temperature under heavy workloads.

While these leaked photos don’t show much beyond what’s already been circulating in rumor reports, they’ve added new fuel to the pre-launch buzz. Physical sightings of unreleased iPhones remain rare, especially this close to Apple’s usual fall release window.

Whether these images actually depict a functioning iPhone 17 Pro or simply a test mule housed in decoy hardware, they’ve succeeded in bringing renewed attention to Apple’s next flagship. And if the design changes are real, they mark one of the more substantial visual shifts in recent years, assuming Apple doesn’t change course at the last minute.

Our Take

If Apple’s aiming to shake up the look and feel of its premium iPhones, these changes could be a step in that direction. But it’s also worth asking: will the external redesign offer enough day-to-day benefit to justify the hype? For now, the details remain fuzzy, literally and figuratively.

Curious what you make of it? Are these leaks enough to get your attention, or just another pre-launch decoy? Sound off in the comments.

keyPoints.title: Alleged iPhone 17 Pro Prototype Surfaces in Los Angeles
keyPoints.explanation: Low-quality photos shared on Twitter appear to show a man holding what looks like a prototype of the iPhone 17 Pro, with some design elements visible, hinting at upcoming changes.

keyPoints.title: Design Elements and Security Measures in Leaked Photos
keyPoints.explanation: The bulky case on the prototype seems intentionally designed to hide details, but features like a rectangular camera bar, LiDAR scanner, and attempts by security personnel to shield the device are notable.

keyPoints.title: Expected Features Based on Rumors and Leaks
keyPoints.explanation: Leaks suggest the iPhone 17 Pro will have a wide, rectangular camera bar, a repositioned Apple logo, a 48MP telephoto lens, anti-reflective coating, new A19 Pro chip, and vapor chamber cooling.

keyPoints.title: Rarity of Physical Sightings and the Impact of Leaks
keyPoints.explanation: Physical sightings of unreleased iPhones are rare at this stage, but these leaks have fueled pre-launch buzz and highlight possible significant visual and technical updates.

keyPoints.title: Editorial Perspective on the Rumored Changes
keyPoints.explanation: While these leaks suggest a major redesign, their actual impact and whether the changes will benefit users enough to justify the hype remains uncertain.
